title: Outliers I - Detection and the Z-Score Method
abstract:
What an outlier is, when it must be removed and when removing it destroys the
problem, which algorithms are damaged by outliers and which are indifferent, the
two treatment strategies (trimming and capping), and the first of the four
detection techniques: Z-score treatment. This document derives the
$\mu\pm3\sigma$ rule from the empirical rule, shows exactly when it is valid,
and demonstrates the two failure modes — skewed data and masking — that make
practitioners reach for the IQR method of Topic 29 instead.

blocks.t: What an Outlier Is
From the notes
A data point different from all other points.

items:
In a few cases outliers need not be removed — e.g. for
 anomaly detection problems.

Linear Regression, Logistic Regression, AdaBoost, Deep Learning
 are all weight-based algorithms, so outliers have a
 high impact there.

blocks.t: The first question is always "is it an error or a fact?"
Three different things get called outliers, and they need different treatment:

head: Kind
Example
Treatment

A real ₹$50$M salary; a real fraud
Corporate accounts mixed into a retail dataset

blocks.t: Statistics cannot tell these apart. Only domain knowledge can.
Never remove outliers from an anomaly-detection problem

The notes flag this explicitly. In fraud detection, defect detection or
predictive maintenance, the outliers are the target. Applying a routine
outlier-removal step deletes every positive case and leaves you with a model that
has never seen the thing it is supposed to find. Check the target's relationship
to the outliers before removing anything.
Which algorithms care

head: Sensitivity
Algorithms
Why
rows: Logistic Regression, AdaBoost, Deep Learning, PCA
Weight-based: a squared error grows quadratically, so one distant point dominates the loss
Distance-based: an extreme coordinate dominates every distance
Split on rank order; a value of $10^6$ is just "bigger than the threshold"

blocks.t: Why squared loss is so vulnerable

Least squares minimises $\sum_i (y_i-\hat y_i)^2$. The gradient contribution of
point $i$ is proportional to its residual $r_i$, so a point with $r_i=100$ pulls
the fit one hundred times harder than a point with $r_i=1$. A single sufficiently
distant point can move the fitted line arbitrarily far — least squares has a
breakdown point of 0.

AdaBoost is worse still: it up-weights misclassified points at every
round (Topic 65), so a mislabelled outlier receives exponentially growing
attention and can consume the entire ensemble.

Absolute loss $\sum|y_i-\hat y_i|$ has a constant gradient and is far more
robust, which is why MAE and quantile regression are the standard defences.
Treating Outliers

blocks.cap:
The two strategies from the notes. Trimming deletes the rows; capping
 keeps every row but clips its value to a boundary.

head: Trimming (remove them)
Capping
rows: Replace the value with the cap
Keeps every row and every other column's data
Creates a spike at the cap value
The value is a genuine error
The value is real but extreme

blocks.t: From the notes, on capping

As an outlier is always on the left or right side, set a cap and say
anything outside those caps on each side takes the value of that cap.
Capping is usually the right default

Trimming throws away the whole row — including all the other columns'
perfectly good values — because of one extreme entry. On a wide dataset that
compounds exactly as complete-case analysis does (Topic 23). Capping keeps the
row, keeps the ordering (the largest value is still the largest), and bounds the
influence. Its only cost is an artificial spike at the boundary.
The Four Detection Techniques
Z-Score Treatment
From the notes
Assumption: the column is normally distributed. This means that:

So anything beyond $\mu+3\sigma$ (upper limit) or $\mu-3\sigma$ (lower
limit) is an outlier.
This is derived from the Z-score formula: $\;z_i = \dfrac{x_i-\mu}{\sigma}$.

blocks.cap:
The empirical rule. The three bands are 68%, 95.4% and 99.7%; the
 red tails beyond $3\sigma$ hold just 0.27% of a normal distribution, which is
 why that boundary is the conventional cut.

blocks.t: The rule, precisely

For $X\sim\mathcal N(\mu,\sigma^2)$ define $z=(x-\mu)/\sigma$, so
$z\sim\mathcal N(0,1)$. Then
Flag $x_i$ as an outlier when $|z_i| > 3$, i.e.
\boxed{ x_i < \mu-3\sigma \quad\text{or}\quad x_i > \mu+3\sigma }

On genuinely normal data this flags $0.27\%$ of points — about 27 in every
10{,}000. That is the false-positive rate you are accepting, and it is
why $3$ rather than $2$ is the usual choice: at $|z|>2$ you would flag 4.6% of
perfectly ordinary data.
Capping with the Z-score rule

The same boundaries serve for capping: clip everything below $\mu-3\sigma$ up to
$\mu-3\sigma$, and everything above $\mu+3\sigma$ down to $\mu+3\sigma$. This is
the "normal data" branch of end-of-distribution imputation in Topic 24 — the
same two numbers, used for a different purpose.
Where the Z-Score Method Fails

blocks.cap:
Left: on normal data the method behaves exactly as theory predicts.
 Middle: on skewed data the rule is meaningless — everything flagged sits on
 one side, and the lower bound may be below the data's minimum. Right: masking
 — as more extreme points are added, $\sigma$ inflates and the method detects
 fewer of them.

blocks.t: Failure 1 — the normality assumption

The rule is derived from the normal distribution. On a right-skewed column like
income, $\mu+3\sigma$ can sit beyond any observed value (flagging nothing) while
$\mu-3\sigma$ falls below zero (flagging nothing on the left either) — or, on
heavier tails, it flags a large fraction of perfectly ordinary high earners.
Test for normality, or transform the column first (Topics 18–19), or
use the IQR method (Topic 29).
Failure 2 — masking

$\mu$ and $\sigma$ are computed from data that includes the outliers, and
both have a breakdown point of 0 (Topic 14). Adding extreme points inflates
$\sigma$, which widens the $3\sigma$ boundary, which lets those same points fall
inside it. A cluster of outliers hides itself.

The standard fix is a robust Z-score built from the median and the median
absolute deviation:

z^{\text{robust}}_i = \frac{0.6745 (x_i-\tilde x)}{\text{MAD}},
 \qquad \text{MAD}=\operatorname{median}\big(|x_i-\tilde x|\big),

where $0.6745$ makes MAD a consistent estimator of $\sigma$ under normality.
Both $\tilde x$ and MAD have a 50% breakdown point, so masking cannot occur.
Fit the boundaries on train only

$\mu$ and $\sigma$ are learned parameters. Compute them on the training set and
apply the same boundaries to test and to production — exactly as with a
scaler. Recomputing them on test would give the two sets different definitions of
"outlier".
Code

import numpy as np, pandas as pd
from scipy import stats
from sklearn.base import BaseEstimator, TransformerMixin
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression, HuberRegressor
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeRegressor
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score, train_test_split

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

# =====================================================================
# 1. WHY OUTLIERS MATTER SO MUCH TO WEIGHT-BASED MODELS
# =====================================================================
x = rng.uniform(0, 10, 200)
y = 2.5 * x + 3 + rng.normal(0, 1.5, 200)

x_out = np.r_[x, [1.0, 2.0, 1.5]]          # 3 points, wildly wrong y
y_out = np.r_[y, [60.0, 65.0, 58.0]]

clean = LinearRegression().fit(x.reshape(-1,1), y)
dirty = LinearRegression().fit(x_out.reshape(-1,1), y_out)
print(f"clean fit: slope {clean.coef_[0]:.3f}  intercept {clean.intercept_:.3f}")
print(f"3 outliers: slope {dirty.coef_[0]:.3f}  intercept {dirty.intercept_:.3f}")
# 3 points out of 203 (1.5%) move the slope by ~40%.

# A TREE barely notices -- it splits on rank order
t1 = DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=3, random_state=0).fit(x.reshape(-1,1), y)
t2 = DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=3, random_state=0).fit(x_out.reshape(-1,1), y_out)
grid = np.linspace(0, 10, 50).reshape(-1, 1)
print("tree prediction change:", np.abs(t1.predict(grid) - t2.predict(grid)).mean().round(3))
print("linear prediction change:", np.abs(clean.predict(grid) - dirty.predict(grid)).mean().round(3))

# A ROBUST loss also resists them:
hub = HuberRegressor(epsilon=1.35).fit(x_out.reshape(-1,1), y_out)
print(f"Huber slope on dirty data: {hub.coef_[0]:.3f}  (true = 2.5)")

# =====================================================================
# 2. THE EMPIRICAL RULE, VERIFIED
# =====================================================================
d = rng.normal(50, 10, 200_000)
for k in [1, 2, 3]:
    inside = np.mean(np.abs(d - d.mean()) <= k * d.std())
    print(f"within {k} sigma: {inside:.4%}   (theory "
          f"{stats.norm.cdf(k)-stats.norm.cdf(-k):.4%})")

# =====================================================================
# 3. Z-SCORE TREATMENT -- detection, trimming, capping
# =====================================================================
income = rng.normal(60_000, 15_000, 5000)
income[rng.choice(5000, 12, replace=False)] = rng.uniform(300_000, 500_000, 12)

mu, sigma = income.mean(), income.std()
lower, upper = mu - 3*sigma, mu + 3*sigma
z = (income - mu) / sigma
outlier = np.abs(z) > 3

print(f"\nmu {mu:,.0f}   sigma {sigma:,.0f}")
print(f"limits: [{lower:,.0f}, {upper:,.0f}]")
print(f"flagged: {outlier.sum()} rows ({outlier.mean():.2%})")

trimmed = income[~outlier]                            # TRIMMING: fast, loses rows
capped  = np.clip(income, lower, upper)               # CAPPING: keeps every row

print(f"trimming: {len(income)} -> {len(trimmed)} rows")
print(f"capping : {len(capped)} rows, {np.sum(capped != income)} values changed")
print(f"std  original {income.std():,.0f}  trimmed {trimmed.std():,.0f}  "
      f"capped {capped.std():,.0f}")

# =====================================================================
# 4. FAILURE 1 -- THE NORMALITY ASSUMPTION
# =====================================================================
skewed = rng.lognormal(3, 0.9, 5000)
m, s = skewed.mean(), skewed.std()
print(f"\nSKEWED column, skew = {stats.skew(skewed):.2f}")
print(f"  mu-3sigma = {m-3*s:8.1f}   but the minimum is {skewed.min():.1f} "
      f"-> flags NOTHING on the left")
print(f"  mu+3sigma = {m+3*s:8.1f}   flags {np.mean(skewed > m+3*s):.2%} "
      f"-- ALL on one side")
_, p = stats.normaltest(skewed)
print(f"  normality test p = {p:.2e} -> the assumption is violated; use IQR (Topic 29)")

# The correct move: transform FIRST, then apply the rule
logged = np.log(skewed)
zl = (logged - logged.mean()) / logged.std()
print(f"  after log transform: skew {stats.skew(logged):+.2f}, "
      f"flagged {np.mean(np.abs(zl) > 3):.2%} -- now symmetric")

# =====================================================================
# 5. FAILURE 2 -- MASKING
# =====================================================================
base = rng.normal(50, 5, 300)
print(f"\n{'planted':>8s} {'sigma':>8s} {'flagged':>8s}")
for k in [0, 1, 3, 10, 30]:
    dd = np.r_[base, [400.0]*k] if k else base
    zz = (dd - dd.mean()) / dd.std()
    print(f"{k:8d} {dd.std():8.1f} {np.sum(np.abs(zz)>3):8d}")
# 1 planted outlier is caught. 30 planted outliers inflate sigma so much
# that NONE of them is caught. They mask each other.

# =====================================================================
# 6. THE ROBUST Z-SCORE -- immune to masking
# =====================================================================
def robust_z(a):
    med = np.median(a)
    mad = np.median(np.abs(a - med))
    return 0.6745 * (a - med) / (mad + 1e-12)   # 0.6745 = Phi^-1(0.75)

for k in [0, 1, 3, 10, 30]:
    dd = np.r_[base, [400.0]*k] if k else base
    print(f"planted {k:3d}: classic z flags {np.sum(np.abs((dd-dd.mean())/dd.std())>3):3d}, "
          f"robust z flags {np.sum(np.abs(robust_z(dd))>3):3d}")
# The robust version catches all of them, every time.

# =====================================================================
# 7. AS A PIPELINE TRANSFORMER, FITTED ON TRAIN ONLY
# =====================================================================
class ZScoreCapper(BaseEstimator, TransformerMixin):
    """Cap at mu +/- k*sigma. Boundaries are LEARNED from training data."""
    def __init__(self, k=3.0, robust=False):
        self.k, self.robust = k, robust

    def fit(self, X, y=None):
        X = np.asarray(X, dtype=float)
        if self.robust:
            centre = np.nanmedian(X, axis=0)
            spread = np.nanmedian(np.abs(X - centre), axis=0) / 0.6745
        else:
            centre = np.nanmean(X, axis=0)
            spread = np.nanstd(X, axis=0)
        self.lower_ = centre - self.k * spread
        self.upper_ = centre + self.k * spread
        return self

    def transform(self, X):
        return np.clip(np.asarray(X, dtype=float), self.lower_, self.upper_)

    def get_feature_names_out(self, input_features=None):
        return np.asarray(input_features, dtype=object)

X = np.c_[income, rng.normal(35, 8, 5000)]
y = (0.00003 * income + rng.normal(0, 1, 5000) > 2).astype(int)
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=.25, random_state=0)

from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
for name, steps in [
    ("no capping", [("sc", StandardScaler())]),
    ("z-score cap", [("cap", ZScoreCapper(3.0)), ("sc", StandardScaler())]),
    ("robust cap",  [("cap", ZScoreCapper(3.0, robust=True)), ("sc", StandardScaler())]),
]:
    pipe = Pipeline(steps + [("clf", LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000))])
    print(f"{name:12s} cv auc "
          f"{cross_val_score(pipe, X_tr, y_tr, cv=5, scoring='roc_auc').mean():.4f}")

capper = ZScoreCapper(3.0).fit(X_tr)
print("\nboundaries learned from TRAIN:", capper.upper_.round(0))
# These SAME numbers are applied to test and to production. Recomputing them
# on test would give the two sets different definitions of "outlier".

# =====================================================================
# 8. CHECK BEFORE YOU DELETE: are the outliers the TARGET?
# =====================================================================
print("\ntarget rate | normal rows :", y[~outlier].mean().round(3))
print("target rate | outlier rows:", y[outlier].mean().round(3))
# If the second number is much higher, you are looking at an anomaly-detection
# problem and removing the outliers deletes every positive case.
Worked Examples
Z-score detection, and why it can miss an outlier
Step 1 – mean and standard deviation (population).
\mu = \frac{127}{9} \approx 14.11, \qquad \sigma \approx 9.18
Step 2 – z-score of the suspicious point 40.
Step 3 – apply the $\pm 3\sigma$ rule. $|2.82| < 3$, so $40$ is not flagged.

Why. The outlier inflates $\mu$ and $\sigma$ itself. Its own z-score is pulled down by the very spread it created (the "masking" effect). With only nine points, one extreme value dominates both statistics. This is the central weakness of z-score treatment, and the reason the IQR method (next chapter), which uses quartiles, is preferred for skewed or small data.
Summary
Everything on one page

items: An outlier is a data point different from all other points.

In a few cases outliers need not be removed — above all for
 anomaly detection, where they are the target.

Linear Regression, Logistic Regression, AdaBoost and Deep
 Learning are weight-based, so outliers have a high impact. Trees are
 largely indifferent; they split on rank order.

Treating outliers: Trimming (remove them) — pro:
 fast; con: reduces data size. Capping — set a cap on each side
 and give anything outside it the value of that cap.

Four detection techniques: Z-score treatment, IQR based
 filtering, Percentile, Winsorization.

Z-score assumes the column is normally distributed: 68% within
 $\mu\pm\sigma$, 95% within $\mu\pm2\sigma$, so anything beyond
 $\mu\pm3\sigma$ is an outlier. Derived from $z_i=(x_i-\mu)/\sigma$.

It flags $0.27\%$ of genuinely normal data — that is the false-positive
 rate you accept.

Two failure modes: it is invalid on skewed data, and it suffers
 masking — outliers inflate $\sigma$ and hide each other.

Fix masking with the robust Z-score using median and MAD; fix
 skew by transforming first or by using the IQR method.
$\mu$ and $\sigma$ are learned parameters: fit on train only.

blocks.t: Questions you will actually be asked
Q. Should you always remove outliers?

No. First decide whether the point is a data error, a genuine rare event, or a
different population. Errors get fixed or removed; genuine rare events are often
the signal — in fraud or defect detection they are the entire target; different
populations should be segmented, not deleted.
Q. Why are linear models so much more sensitive than trees?

Squared loss weights a point by its residual, so influence grows without bound
and least squares has a breakdown point of zero. A tree only asks whether a value
falls above or below a threshold, so an extreme value is simply "large".
Q. Trimming or capping?

Capping is usually better: it keeps the row, and therefore all the other
columns' good values, while bounding the influence. Trimming is faster but
reduces the data size, and on a wide dataset the row loss compounds. Trim when
the value is genuinely an error.
Q. What is masking?

Outliers hiding each other. $\mu$ and $\sigma$ are computed from data that
includes them, so a cluster of extreme points inflates $\sigma$, widening the
$3\sigma$ boundary until those same points fall inside it. Use the robust
Z-score — median and MAD — which cannot be moved by up to half the data.
Q. Your income column is right-skewed. Can you use the Z-score rule?

Not directly. The rule assumes normality; on skewed data $\mu-3\sigma$ can fall
below the minimum while $\mu+3\sigma$ flags ordinary high earners. Either
log-transform the column first and then apply the rule, or use the IQR method,
which makes no distributional assumption.
Q. Why 3 sigma rather than 2?

Because $|z|>2$ flags 4.6% of genuinely normal data — one row in 22, which is
an unacceptable false-positive rate for a routine cleaning step. $|z|>3$ flags
0.27%.
